prompt: The programs on the shop's server were quietly replaced. No data file changed. Which property was lost?

choices.text: Availability, since the server is no longer the same
choices.why: The server still answers. Nothing says it stopped working.

choices.text: Integrity
choices.why: Right. Integrity covers the systems as well as the data in them.

choices.text: Privacy of the staff
choices.why: Privacy concerns the people data describes; no personal data is involved here.

choices.text: Confidentiality of the program files
choices.why: Nobody is said to have read anything secret.

prompt: For the shop's front page, which property does the lesson rank first?

choices.text: Availability
choices.why: Right. It is public by design; when it is down, no book sells.

choices.text: Confidentiality, because the page shows the catalogue
choices.why: The page is public by design; hiding it would defeat its purpose.

choices.text: Integrity, then confidentiality
choices.why: That pairing is not the one the lesson gives for the front page.

choices.text: Non-repudiation of each visit
choices.why: Proving who visited is beside the point for a public page.

prompt: sha256sum -c reports FAILED for prices.csv. What has ana learnt at this point?

choices.text: That the file differs from when its fingerprint was saved
choices.why: Right. A hash says that something changed, not what or who.

choices.text: That the price list leaked
choices.why: A leak is about who read it; the check is about whether bytes changed.

choices.text: That somebody tampered with the second line of the price list
choices.why: A hash points at no line and says nothing about intent.

choices.text: Which user edited the file and when
choices.why: Finding out who and when is a separate job.

prompt: The shop keeps a backup drive with the customer list in a desk drawer. Which property does that extra copy put at risk?

choices.text: Confidentiality
choices.why: Right. Every copy is one more place for the data to leak from.

choices.text: Accountability of the owners
choices.why: The issue is where the data sits, not tracing actions to people.

choices.text: Integrity of the database
choices.why: Keeping a copy changes nothing in the database.

choices.text: Availability, since a drawer is hard to reach
choices.why: A copy helps availability; it is the leak side that suffers.

prompt: Three staff send orders from a chat channel where everybody signs in with one shared password. A supplier disputes an order. What is the channel unable to give?

choices.text: Integrity, since a chat message is easy to edit
choices.why: Nothing says the text changed; the question is who wrote it.

choices.text: Availability of the order
choices.why: The order is there; the dispute is about who sent it.

choices.text: Non-repudiation: proof of who sent it
choices.why: Right. A message anybody with the shared password could have sent has no non-repudiation.

choices.text: Confidentiality of the chat
choices.why: The messages may be private and still prove nothing about the sender.

prompt: The Parkerian hexad adds a property for data that is there and useless, like an encrypted file with no key. That property is ___.
In the lesson's vocabulary, what is an exploit?

choices.text: The person or group behind an attack
choices.why: That is a threat actor.

choices.text: The concrete method, tool or code that uses a weakness
choices.why: Right. The exploit is how a vulnerability is taken advantage of.

choices.text: The weakness in a program or a configuration that an attacker uses
choices.why: That is the vulnerability, not the exploit.

choices.text: A threat that has turned into an incident
choices.why: That is an incident, the event itself.

prompt: Why does the lesson say accidental threats deserve more respect than they get?

choices.text: Most attackers disguise their work as accidents
choices.why: The lesson says nothing of the kind.

choices.text: Accidents are covered by insurance and attacks are not
choices.why: Insurance is not the lesson's argument here.

choices.text: A mistake is not deterred and does not get bored
choices.why: Right. A mistake has no intention, so the thought of being caught does not stop it.

choices.text: Accidents cost the shop more than attacks do
choices.why: The lesson makes no such comparison of cost.

prompt: According to the lesson, what makes the insider dangerous as a threat actor?

choices.text: Insiders are the most skilled attackers there are
choices.why: The lesson gives the most capability to nation-states.

choices.text: They use automated tools against the whole internet
choices.why: That describes the opportunistic criminal.

choices.text: They want attention for a cause
choices.why: That describes a hacktivist.

choices.text: They already have access
choices.why: Right. Accounts, keys and the trust of colleagues are already theirs.

prompt: A flaw has a CVSS score of 6.9. In which band does it fall?

choices.text: medium
choices.why: Right. Medium runs from 4.0 to 6.9.

choices.text: high
choices.why: High starts at 7.0.

choices.text: low
choices.why: Low ends at 3.9.

choices.text: critical
choices.why: Critical starts at 9.0.

prompt: In the identifier CVE-2021-44228, what does 2021 tell you?

choices.text: The version of the affected library
choices.why: A CVE is a name, not a version number.

choices.text: The year the flaw was first exploited
choices.why: The identifier records nothing about exploitation.

choices.text: The year the number was given out
choices.why: Right. The year of assignment, then a sequence number.

choices.text: Its severity score on a hidden scale
choices.why: Severity is the CVSS score, a separate thing.

prompt: Of the four questions that move likelihood, which does the lesson say are in a defender's hands? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: motivation: whether anybody is looking
choices.why: A shop cannot make criminals less motivated.

choices.text: history: how often it happened before
choices.why: History is evidence for an estimate, not one of the four levers.

choices.text: exposure: who reaches the weakness
choices.why: Right. The shop decides whether the portal is reachable from the internet.

choices.text: existing controls: what stands in the way
choices.why: Right. Adding MFA or a firewall rule is in the shop's hands.

prompt: "The website may be down for at most four hours a month." Which term does the lesson give that kind of statement?

choices.text: residual risk
choices.why: Residual risk is what remains after controls.

choices.text: risk tolerance
choices.why: Right. Tolerance is where the policy meets a measurement.

choices.text: risk appetite
choices.why: Appetite is the overall policy set by leadership, not a number for one objective.

choices.text: inherent risk
choices.why: Inherent risk is the risk before any control.

prompt: The shop wrote its register once and filed it two years ago. What does the lesson say that document now is?

choices.text: A list of scanner findings to fix
choices.why: A register is not a list of findings at all.

choices.text: A finished assessment that auditors prefer
choices.why: The frameworks the lesson names require the review.

choices.text: A snapshot of a shop that no longer exists
choices.why: Right. Risks move, which is why the review date is a promise.

choices.text: A valid record until an incident proves it wrong
choices.why: Waiting for an incident is exactly what the review date avoids.

prompt: Which treatment did the shop choose for R2, ransomware?

choices.text: Transfer it to the payment provider

choices.text: Mitigate and transfer

choices.text: Accept, signed by the owners
choices.why: That is R5, the flood.

choices.text: corrective

prompt: What does the lesson say a layer nobody maintains becomes?

choices.text: A harmless extra layer at no cost
choices.why: The lesson says layers have costs and decay.

choices.text: A hole with a reassuring name

choices.text: A compensating control waiting to be written down

prompt: What does the lesson say training does for the fake invoice email?

choices.text: It is a physical control in the lesson's grid
choices.why: Training is administrative.

choices.text: It lowers the chance of a click; inner layers still matter

choices.text: It makes the inner layers behind it unnecessary for that email
choices.why: The inner layers still matter because training has holes too.

choices.text: It detects the email after it is opened
choices.why: Training works before the click, not as detection.

prompt: Which of these are technical controls, in the lesson's classification by nature? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: file permissions

choices.text: VLANs

choices.text: Donn Parker

prompt: Why do job rotation and mandatory vacations help against fraud?

choices.why: That is about access, not about who does the job.

choices.why: Training is not the reason the lesson gives.

prompt: Why does the lesson say privilege creep is quiet by nature?

choices.text: Access reviews are run by IT, which sees little
choices.why: The lesson has the data's owner run the review.

choices.text: The logs hide extra permissions from the owners
choices.why: The lesson blames no log; the problem is that nobody looks.

choices.text: It affects new joiners, who do not know their rights
choices.why: Creep grows on long-serving people, not new ones.

choices.text: Too much access breaks no task
choices.why: Right. So nobody complains, and it shows up in an incident.

prompt: Which of these are ways the lesson says privilege creep builds up? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: someone moves from support to finance with support's access attached
choices.why: Right. The mover's old access was never removed.

choices.text: a joiner receives the role's standard access on day one
choices.why: That is the correct joiner process, not creep.

choices.text: a project ends and its shared folder stays shared
choices.why: Right. The reason ended and the access did not.

choices.text: a person covers for a colleague on holiday and keeps the access
choices.why: Right. Access granted for a reason outlives the reason.

choices.text: ana steps up to root through a just-in-time grant
choices.why: Just-in-time access is removed afterwards; it is a defence against creep.

prompt: In SP 800-207, which component judges a request against the rules?

choices.text: The policy administrator
choices.why: It passes the result on; it does not evaluate.

choices.text: The enforcement point
choices.why: The PEP asks and acts; it decides nothing itself.

choices.text: The policy engine
choices.why: Right. The administrator then tells the PEP the result.

prompt: A member of staff works from home with her own correct password. How does a location-based policy treat her?

choices.text: As staff, once the firewall logs her address
choices.why: Logging an address grants nothing here.

choices.text: As a contractor with reduced rights
choices.why: The policy has no such middle category.

choices.text: Like a stranger, since she is outside

prompt: Under Zero Trust, what happens to traffic between two internal machines?

choices.why: The identity provider supplies a signal, not a route.

choices.text: It is blocked unless a VPN carries it
choices.why: The VPN is not what Zero Trust relies on.

choices.text: It is encrypted, as outside connections are
choices.why: Right. Part of assuming breach.

choices.text: It is left in clear, since both are inside
choices.why: That is trust by location again.

prompt: How does the lesson suggest checking whether a change really moved an organisation to Zero Trust?

choices.text: Confirm that a vendor's gateway sits in front of the payroll
choices.why: A product in place proves nothing on its own.

choices.text: Turn off the firewall and watch whether anything breaks
choices.why: The firewall stays as a layer.

choices.text: the policy administrator

choices.text: The identity half

choices.text: The logging half

prompt: Which weakness does the lesson give for discretionary access control?

choices.text: Owners share freely and forget to unshare

prompt: SELinux and AppArmor are a form of which model, inside operating systems?

choices.text: Attribute-based access control

choices.text: Discretionary access control
